instructions:
## The project being researched

An XGBoost "virtual sensor" for Iowa stream nitrate: predict at locations with NO physical sensor, using only weather + land-use data. Two targets:
- REGRESSION: daily-max nitrate concentration (mg/L)
- CLASSIFICATION (the primary one): binary `violation` = daily max >= 10 mg/L, base rate 0.263

~85 sensor sites, 160,074 site-days, 2008-2026. Each site has a delineated upstream drainage basin. Features are aggregated over basin cells in distance buckets from the outlet.

## THE DEPLOYMENT TARGET - judge every recommendation against this
The shipped product takes an ARBITRARY MAP PIN anywhere in Iowa, delineates its upstream basin on the fly via USGS NLDI, builds features from weather and land use alone, and predicts daily violation probability. There is NO nitrate history at the target location, NO discharge gauge there, and NO guarantee of a monitored neighbor upstream. Any method that requires the target site's own observations, or requires a gauged upstream site, DOES NOT WORK for this product - it may still be useful for other purposes, but that limitation must be stated explicitly and prominently.

## Current honest performance (leave-one-basin-family-out, LOFO)
- CLF: AUC 0.820, PR-AUC 0.634 (2.41x lift over base rate), recall 0.524 at 10% false-alarm rate, MCC 0.466, Brier 0.137
- REG: R2 0.328, RMSE 4.36 mg/L
- Deployed at beta=2: recall 0.864, but 59% of alarms are false

## THE CENTRAL PROBLEM: the model cannot rank sites
- within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21
- macro_auc 0.90 vs between_rate_r2 0.24
The project's own summary: "a good timer, a mediocre site-ranker." It captures WHEN nitrate rises at a given site, but fails at the ABSOLUTE LEVEL of an unseen basin. Essentially all remaining headroom is in the between-site term.

## CRITICAL SAMPLE-SIZE CONSTRAINT
The ~85 sites collapse to only 19 INDEPENDENT BASIN FAMILIES under the leak-safe CV (sites whose basins nest and whose records overlap in time are grouped). So learning a site's absolute level is a regression with roughly 19 effective independent units, NOT 160k rows. Any method whose published gains come from hundreds of catchments (e.g. CAMELS with 531-671 basins) must be explicitly flagged as possibly infeasible here.

## Current features (68 for CLF)
9 weather variables x 3 distance buckets (SAME-DAY SCALARS ONLY), 8 CDL crop classes x 3 buckets, 2 nitrogen-surplus x 3 buckets, doy_sin/doy_cos, 4 cross-site nitrate lags (rest_of_state_nitrate_lag1/2/3/5), 5 static (lat, lon, log_basin_area, mean_dist_to_sensor, max_dist_to_sensor).
Top features by permutation importance: rest_of_state_nitrate_lag1, lon, lat, doy_sin, fuel_moisture_1000h. BOTTOM: all daily weather; precip_in_1d is dead last (perm ~0.000).

## KNOWN NEGATIVE RESULTS - do not naively re-propose these
- Lagged weather copies: HURT badly (loso_r2 0.116 -> 0.019)
- Rolling precip / water balance as implemented: worse (lofo_r2 0.013 vs 0.003)
- Broadcasting 2017 N-surplus forward in time: much worse (-0.166)
- Rolling (3D/7D) smoothed targets: worse
- Spike / anomaly z-score targets: failed cross-site (lofo_r2 ~ -0.0006)
- Antecedent moisture + rain x surplus interactions: REG a wash, CLF only +0.017 PR-AUC
- Riparian 0-2km bucket: CLF +0.039 PR-AUC but REG worse
- Advective travel-time routing IS ALREADY IMPLEMENTED (weather per distance bucket shifted by median flow distance / 2.1 m/s) and is part of the "lagged weather hurt" failure.
PATTERN: nearly every hydrologically-motivated TEMPORAL feature has failed. The only wins came from geometry and static geography. This strongly suggests the deficit is in BETWEEN-SITE static information, not in temporal dynamics.

## Data present on disk but UNUSED
- discharge/streamflow: only 22 of 85 sites (all USGS, 0.66-0.97 density, up to 18 years). ZERO of the 61 IWQIS sites.
- co-located water chemistry: specific conductance (65 sites), water temp (80), pH (64), dissolved oxygen (64), turbidity + phosphate (61)
- upstream_uid (28 sites) / downstream_uid (40 sites) river-network topology: completely unread
- draining_area (80/85), NHDPlus comid (stored per basin), basin containment graph (used only to build CV folds)

## Known data problems
- Nitrogen surplus (gTREND product) ENDS IN 2017 -> NaN for 68% of training rows
- 16.5% of grid cells lack crop/surplus data; an inner join silently UNDER-COUNTS crop area and N surplus for basins extending outside Iowa (worst for the largest multi-state basins)
- Tile drainage density: known to be the dominant hydrologic control in Iowa, NOT in the feature set, and NO data source has been identified yet


## Non-negotiable rules for this research

1. RECORD THE SPLIT PROTOCOL FOR EVERY PERFORMANCE NUMBER, AND DO NOT COMPARE NUMBERS ACROSS PROTOCOLS. Random-split results are valid evidence about method behavior and should be reported - researchers using them often have good reasons for their own question. But only SPATIALLY HELD-OUT numbers (leave-one-basin-out, leave-one-region-out, ungauged-basin protocol) are comparable to our LOFO 0.820, because a random split over autocorrelated site-days lets a model memorize a site's level and measures interpolation rather than transfer. When the protocol cannot be determined, say so rather than guessing.
2. REPORT EFFECT SIZES AND SAMPLE SIZES, NOT CONCLUSIONS. "GNNs improve water quality prediction" is worthless. "Recurrent GCN, 456 reaches, 42 monitored, held-out-node RMSE 1.83 vs 2.11 for LSTM" is actionable. Always give the number of catchments/basins/sites used.
3. EVERY DATASET RECOMMENDATION MUST BE OPERATIONAL: exact name, spatial resolution, temporal resolution, coverage years, whether it covers ALL of Iowa AND the multi-state portions of basins, exact URL, access mechanism (API/bulk/FTP), authentication requirement, and license.
4. ACTIVELY HUNT FOR NEGATIVE RESULTS. Seven feature-engineering ablations have already failed on this project. Papers reporting that a technique did NOT transfer are as valuable as successes and are systematically under-published - look in discussion/limitations sections and in benchmark comparison papers.
5. FLAG THE n=19-FAMILIES CONSTRAINT against every recommendation. If a method's evidence base comes from 300+ basins, say so explicitly and assess whether it can work at n=19.
6. ACQUISITION CONSTRAINT: recommend only free/public data, or data obtainable by a reasonable request (e.g. emailing IIHR or Iowa DNR). No paid datasets, no field campaigns, no new sensor deployment.
7. Prefer peer-reviewed literature and authoritative agency sources over blog posts. Give DOIs where they exist.
8. JUDGE EVERYTHING AGAINST THE DEPLOYMENT TARGET: an arbitrary ungauged map pin with no local history. State plainly when a method only works at gauged sites.


## Your assignment: synthesize the findings for angle "Exceedance methodology, and whether the prediction target itself is right"

### Research question
Two separate questions. (a) What methods are established for predicting THRESHOLD EXCEEDANCE in environmental time series - direct binary classification vs regression-then-threshold vs distributional-then-integrate, extreme-value / peaks-over-threshold approaches, cost-sensitive and calibrated classification? (b) Is "daily maximum >= 10 mg/L in raw stream water" the target the water-quality literature would actually use?

### What a good answer contains
Evidence on regression-then-threshold vs direct classification for environmental exceedance, with metrics. Whether peaks-over-threshold / extreme value theory is used for water quality. The regulatory definition of the nitrate MCL and its averaging period, and how monitoring and TMDL practice operationalize exceedance for STREAMS as opposed to treated water. Any literature on sensor-derived daily statistics and sampling-frequency bias. Guidance on evaluation metrics for spatially-held-out exceedance prediction, so our 0.82 AUC / 2.41x lift can be compared to published virtual-sensor numbers rather than to nothing.

### TIER 3 - UNVERIFIED claims
These were extracted from real sources but were NEVER adversarially verified - verification was cut to conserve budget. The characteristic failure mode in this corpus is CONFIDENT OVERREACH FROM THIN EVIDENCE, not fabrication: a claim's conclusion is often right while its stated warrant is wrong, its effect size misattributed, or its split protocol misdescribed.

STRICT RULES for tier 3, which you MUST follow:
- USE them for COVERAGE and LEADS: naming a dataset, a URL, an access route, a candidate attribute, or an angle worth pursuing.
- DO NOT use them as the warrant for any numeric performance figure, any effect size, or the core argument of any recommendation. Those must rest on verified (tier 1) claims.
- Any finding that rests on tier 3 MUST set confidence to "unverified" and say so in the claim text itself.
- If a tier 3 claim contradicts a verified claim, the verified claim wins; note the conflict.

Produce the structured finding set for this angle as JSON.

Merge semantic duplicates. Apply every correction supplied by the verifiers. Rank findings by relevance to the BETWEEN-SITE gap specifically. For each finding give feasibilityAtN19 and worksAtUngaugedPin honestly. Populate "datasets" for every concrete data source, with howToIncorporate written concretely enough to act on - name the feature that would be created and how it would be aggregated to a basin. Populate "uncovered" for any part of the question that produced nothing verifiable - absence of evidence must be reported as absence, never silently dropped. Your "verdict" must state plainly whether this angle is worth pursuing and why.

Output JSON with keys: angle, verdict, findings[] (each: claim, confidence, effectSize, splitProtocol, nBasins, sources[], feasibilityAtN19, worksAtUngaugedPin), datasets[] (each: name, url, resolution, years, access, license, coversMultiState, whyUseful, howToIncorporate, limitations), refuted[], uncovered[].
angleTitle: Exceedance methodology, and whether the prediction target itself is right

tier3_unverified.claim: Brenning, Frank & Suesse (2026, Environmental Modelling & Software 204:107097, DOI 10.1016/j.envsoft.2026.107097) report that when spatial models of groundwater nitrate concentration are used for exceedance mapping by thresholding the point predictions, standard interpolation and machine-learning techniques UNDERESTIMATE the total polluted (threshold-exceeding) area by 80%-98%, even though the same models show 'strong concentration-prediction metrics'. This is a direct, quantified argument against the regression-then-threshold pipeline: good R2/RMSE on concentration does not imply unbiased exceedance delineation, because conditional-mean (or kriged) predictions shrink toward the mean and systematically fail to cross the threshold. NOTE: extracted from abstract only - full text was unreachable (Elsevier 403 on both the HTML article and the CC-BY PDF).
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 80%-98% underestimation of exceedance area by thresholding point predictions
tier3_unverified.nBasins: unknown (groundwater wells, national-scale dataset; count not recoverable from abstract; authors are at Friedrich Schiller University Jena so the dataset is most likely German national groundwater monitoring, unverified)

tier3_unverified.claim: The same paper argues the correct framing is to treat exceedance mapping 'as probabilistic prediction rather than thresholding point estimates' - i.e. predict P(concentration >= threshold) directly (or integrate a predictive distribution above the threshold) instead of predicting a concentration and comparing it to the threshold. This is peer-reviewed support for the sustag project's choice to make the binary `violation` classifier the PRIMARY model rather than deriving violations from the R2=0.328 regression. It also implies the regression model should NOT be repurposed as a violation detector by thresholding its output at 10 mg/L without recalibration.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: qualitative methodological claim; supported by the 80-98% area-underestimation result above

tier3_unverified.claim: The paper's core proposed correction is AREA CALIBRATION: 'a calibrated probability threshold that ensures an unbiased delineation of the polluted area', where the total exceedance area is first estimated from the data and the operating probability threshold is then chosen so the predicted positive area matches that estimate. The authors report this 'effectively eliminates this bias and balances omission versus commission errors', and state the method is model-agnostic and applicable to threshold-based environmental decisions generally. For sustag this is a concrete, cheap, testable alternative to the current beta=2 F-beta operating point (recall 0.864 / 59% false alarms): instead of maximizing F-beta, pick the threshold so the predicted violation rate on held-out folds equals the estimated true base rate 0.263, and report omission/commission balance.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: bias 'effectively eliminated'; no numeric residual bias recoverable from abstract

tier3_unverified.claim: The paper introduces 'target-weighted cross-validation' as its evaluation protocol for exceedance mapping - i.e. cross-validation whose error weighting is aligned to the decision target (exceedance area / classification) rather than to squared error on concentration. Whether this CV is SPATIALLY blocked cannot be determined from the abstract; the abstract does not state a spatial-holdout design, so its performance numbers are NOT directly comparable to sustag's LOFO AUC 0.820 / PR-AUC 0.634. (Caveat for the reader: Alexander Brenning is the author of the `sperrorest` R package and a long-standing advocate of spatial cross-validation, so a spatial design is likely but is NOT established by the retrievable metadata.)
tier3_unverified.effectSize: n/a - protocol description

tier3_unverified.claim: The modeling stack in the paper is trans-Gaussian regression-kriging combined with QUANTILE REGRESSION FORESTS, with 'structured non-stationarity across hydrogeological districts' - i.e. district-level (region-level) model structure rather than one global model. Reported ancillary figures: per-district linear model R2 ranges 0.15-0.62 and semivariogram practical ranges 0.3-22.3 km. The quantile-regression-forest component is the 'distributional-then-integrate' route to exceedance probability (fit the full conditional distribution, integrate above the threshold), which is the third of the three candidate approaches and is here used in production alongside geostatistics. Relevance/limit for sustag: the spatial-correlation ranges are 0.3-22.3 km for groundwater wells, far shorter than typical Iowa inter-sensor distances, and the kriging half of the method requires a spatially dense observation network - it will NOT transfer to an arbitrary Iowa map pin whose nearest nitrate sensor may be tens of km away. Only the QRF + area-calibration half is deployable for sustag.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: linear-model R2 0.15-0.62 across districts; semivariogram practical ranges 0.3-22.3 km

tier3_unverified.claim: NEGATIVE / SCOPE FINDING about this source relative to the assignment: this paper does NOT address (a) peaks-over-threshold or extreme-value theory for water quality, (b) the regulatory definition or averaging period of the 10 mg/L nitrate-N MCL, (c) TMDL or stream-monitoring operationalization of exceedance as distinct from treated drinking water, (d) sensor-derived daily statistics or sampling-frequency bias, or (e) published virtual-sensor AUC/PR-AUC benchmarks for spatially held-out exceedance prediction. It is a purely SPATIAL, static-snapshot GROUNDWATER mapping paper with no time-series component, so it supplies no comparator for sustag's 0.820 AUC / 2.41x lift and no guidance on whether 'daily maximum >= 10 mg/L in raw stream water' is the right target. Its transferable content is confined to the estimator-bias and area-calibration argument. Those other questions must be answered from other sources.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: n/a - scope limitation

tier3_unverified.claim: Baggio & Muzy (2026, arXiv:2605.31079) directly test regression/distributional-then-threshold against direct binary classification for environmental threshold exceedance, and find the full-distribution approach (M2: model the complete conditional law of the target, then integrate its tail above the threshold) consistently outperforms direct binary classification (M1) for RARE events, while the two are essentially EQUIVALENT at moderate exceedance probabilities. Reported ratio PSS_1/PSS_2 approaches 1.0 at exceedance probability p=0.2 and falls to roughly 0.65 at p=0.002 for 1-hour-ahead wind speed. Direct implication for this project: our violation base rate is 0.263, which is ABOVE the p=0.2 regime where the paper finds no advantage for the distributional route — so this paper does NOT support switching our primary CLF target from direct binary classification to regression-then-threshold. It would only argue for the switch if we moved to a much rarer threshold (e.g. a 20-30 mg/L alarm, or a rare-percentile site-specific exceedance).
tier3_unverified.effectSize: PSS_1/PSS_2 ~1.0 at p=0.2; ~0.65 at p=0.002. Brier Skill Score: BSS_2 stays positive as p decreases while BSS_1 degrades sharply. Thresholds tested, wind: p in {0.2, 0.1, 0.08, 0.05, 0.03, 0.01, 0.005, 0.002}; rainfall: p in {0.5, 0.4, 0.3, 0.25, 0.2, 0.15, 0.1, 0.05, 0.025}. Results reported graphically (Figs 4-5); no exact numeric tables recoverable, so the 0.65 figure is read off a figure and should be treated as approximate.
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: random-split (random partition of CALENDAR DAYS into 85% train / 10% val / 5% test, with all samples from a day kept together to block within-day autocorrelation leakage). This is a random temporal split, NOT a spatial holdout. Numbers are NOT comparable to our LOFO 0.820 AUC.
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 278 ground stations (wind), 268 stations (rainfall), southeastern France, MeteoNet 2016-2018; ~3.5e6 training samples

tier3_unverified.claim: The paper gives a sample-size argument for why direct binary classification degrades on rare events: the direct classifier's EFFECTIVE sample size is approximately pN (only the exceedance-positive cases carry information about the threshold), whereas the distributional model uses all N observations, since moderate-intensity events still inform the conditional mean and variance. The stated error ratio is E_2/E_1 = O(p). Applied to this project: at base rate 0.263 with 160,074 site-days, effective positive count is ~42,000 events, so the direct classifier is NOT in the data-starved regime this argument describes. The binding constraint here is n=19 independent basin families, which is a between-site degrees-of-freedom problem this paper's theory does not address at all — its efficiency argument is about event rarity within a pooled sample, not about spatial transfer.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Effective sample size pN for direct classification vs N for distributional; error ratio E_2/E_1 = O(p) (Eqs. 24-25). No explicit minimum event count stated.

tier3_unverified.claim: Baggio & Muzy EXPLICITLY REJECT extreme value theory / peaks-over-threshold for this problem. They use no Generalized Pareto Distribution and no POT threshold selection, citing EVT's 'notoriously difficult bias-variance trade-off' in threshold selection, and instead fit full-support parametric conditional distributions: a three-parameter multifractal-Rice (M-Rice) law with parameters (nu, sigma^2, lambda^2) for wind speed, and a zero-inflated mixed lognormal (p_wet, mu, sigma^2) for hourly rainfall. This is a directly relevant negative signal for the research angle: a 2026 paper whose entire subject is threshold exceedance forecasting deliberately declined to use POT/EVT, on the grounds that fitting the bulk and integrating the tail is more stable than fitting the tail directly.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Qualitative methodological choice; no EVT baseline was run, so the paper provides no head-to-head EVT-vs-distributional number.

tier3_unverified.claim: The paper reports that the specific PARAMETRIC SHAPE of the assumed conditional distribution 'plays a secondary role' compared with accurately capturing shifts in the bulk properties (conditional mean and variance) of the distribution. Differences among alternative parametric families are described as 'limited' though not negligible, with a full sensitivity analysis deferred to future work. Implication for this project: if we ever do move to a distributional target for nitrate, the payoff would come from getting the conditional MEAN and VARIANCE right per site-day, not from choosing a fancy heavy-tailed family. That maps directly onto our known deficit — between_r2 0.21 vs within_r2 0.42 means we are failing on the conditional MEAN LEVEL of an unseen basin, which is exactly the quantity the paper says dominates exceedance skill. A distributional reformulation would not fix that; it would inherit the same between-site error.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Qualitative; sensitivity analysis across parametric families explicitly deferred, so the 'secondary role' claim is asserted rather than fully quantified in this paper.

tier3_unverified.claim: CRITICAL LIMITATION for our use case: Baggio & Muzy train a SINGLE POOLED model across all 278 stations with station metadata (latitude, longitude, altitude) as contextual features — architecturally the same trick as our lat/lon/static-geography features — but they NEVER evaluate transfer to unseen stations. Their split partitions calendar days, not stations, so every test-set station was also in training. The paper therefore provides ZERO evidence about the ungauged/unmonitored-location deployment target, which is precisely our product's setting (arbitrary map pin, no local history). Its conclusions about M2 > M1 are established only under station-interpolation conditions and must not be transferred to our LOFO regime without independent validation.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Generalization to unseen locations is unexplored; the authors' own framing is 'at a specific location', i.e. locations with training history.
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: random-split by calendar day; explicitly NOT a spatial/station holdout

tier3_unverified.claim: For evaluation of environmental exceedance forecasts, Baggio & Muzy use a two-tier metric set that is standard in the meteorological verification literature: PROPER SCORING RULES on the probabilistic output (Brier score and logarithmic score, reported as skill scores against climatology, i.e. BSS) plus DETERMINISTIC categorical skill scores after thresholding the probability (Peirce Skill Score, Critical Success Index, Heidke Skill Score). Notably they do NOT report ROC-AUC or PR-AUC as headline metrics. Implication for this project: our current reporting (AUC 0.820, PR-AUC 0.634, 2.41x lift, Brier 0.137) is missing the climatology-referenced skill scores that this literature treats as the comparison standard. Converting our Brier 0.137 to a Brier Skill Score against the base-rate-0.263 climatological forecast (whose Brier is 0.263*0.737 = 0.1938) gives BSS = 1 - 0.137/0.1938 = 0.293, and adding PSS/CSI/HSS at our operating points would make our numbers directly comparable to the meteorological exceedance-forecasting literature instead of incomparable.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Metric set: Brier score, logarithmic score, BSS, Peirce Skill Score, CSI, HSS. The BSS = 0.293 figure is our own arithmetic from our Brier 0.137 and base rate 0.263, not a number from the paper.
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: random-split by calendar day (their numbers); our derived BSS 0.293 is spatial-holdout (LOFO) and the two must not be compared

tier3_unverified.claim: Zero-shot spatial transfer of an exceedance classifier collapsed to near-chance. Random Forest models trained on one city's beaches and applied to another city's beaches with NO target-site data scored AUC 0.567 (Chicago source -> San Diego target) and AUC 0.482 (San Diego -> Chicago), versus AUC 0.733 and 0.607 for same-region models. The authors describe the San Diego -> Chicago generalization as 'no better than chance alone' (AUC 0.482). DIRECT RELEVANCE: this is the closest published analogue to our deployment target (arbitrary ungauged pin, no local history), and it says between-site/between-region absolute-level transfer is exactly where these models break — consistent with our within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21. Our LOFO AUC 0.820 is ABOVE every cross-region number in this paper, though the comparison is imperfect (different analyte, and their spatial units are two whole metro regions rather than 19 basin families).
tier3_unverified.effectSize: AUC 0.733 (SD local) / 0.607 (Chicago local) vs 0.567 and 0.482 zero-shot cross-region; sensitivity dropped 0.742 -> 0.463 (Chicago->SD) and 0.256 -> 0.208 (SD->Chicago)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 33 beaches total (19 Chicago freshwater, 2016-2019; 14 San Diego marine, 2014-2021); 15,033 beach-days. But transfer was evaluated at the REGION level, so n=2 effective independent transfer units — an even more severe version of our n=19-families constraint, and the authors' own headline finding is that they could not tell which source beaches transfer well.

tier3_unverified.claim: The paper's headline improvement — '28.3% increase in WF1 scores and 5.4% in AUC' — comes from SUPERVISED transfer learning that REQUIRES LABELED OBSERVATIONS AT THE TARGET SITE. The paper states: 'The assumption in supervised TL is that a few samples of labeled target data are provided (in this study, the label is the ENT threshold exceedance).' The two methods that produced the gains (Feature Augmentation FA, Boosting for Weighted Transfer BWT) are supervised; the regularization parameter gamma controls 'the importance attributed to labeled target data.' The number of labeled target samples required is NOT stated. VERDICT AGAINST OUR DEPLOYMENT TARGET: this technique DOES NOT WORK for an arbitrary map pin with no nitrate history. It would only work for adding a NEW MONITORED site after it has accumulated some observations. This must be stated prominently if TL is proposed.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Chicago->SD TL-FA: AUC 0.713, sens 0.729, spec 0.701, WF1 0.680 (vs zero-shot 0.567/0.463/0.620/0.535). SD->Chicago TL-FA: AUC 0.610, sens 0.291, spec 0.825, WF1 0.642 (vs zero-shot 0.482/0.208/0.807/0.408). TL essentially RECOVERED local-model performance (0.713 vs 0.733 local) but did not exceed it.

tier3_unverified.claim: On methodology question (a): this paper provides NO evidence for regression-then-threshold vs direct classification, because it only ever built DIRECT BINARY CLASSIFIERS (Logistic Regression and Random Forest) of threshold exceedance. It did not fit a continuous FIB regression and threshold the prediction, and it used no extreme-value / peaks-over-threshold machinery. This is the field norm for beach nowcasting exceedance work rather than a tested choice. Do not cite this paper as support for our binary CLF target being superior to REG-then-threshold; it is only evidence that direct classification is the ESTABLISHED default in the FIB exceedance literature. Random Forest generally outperformed Logistic Regression across transfer scenarios.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: no head-to-head regression-vs-classification numbers reported

tier3_unverified.claim: PRECEDENT FOR MOVING OUR THRESHOLD: the authors deliberately set the exceedance threshold at 50% OF THE REGULATORY VALUE — 320 CCE/100 mL for Chicago (vs the EPA Beach Action Value of 640, qPCR) and 30 CFU/100 mL for San Diego (vs BAV 60, culture) — justified as 'a more health-protective (conservative) level,' referencing the 2012 EPA Recreational Water Quality Criteria. Their stated reason includes that 'neither Chicago nor San Diego beaches typically approach their respective BAVs,' i.e. the full regulatory threshold produced too few positives to model. The outcome was defined on SINGLE DAILY MEASUREMENTS (Chicago samples collected once daily at 06:00-08:00), with no averaging period. This is a peer-reviewed, ES&T-published precedent for (i) using a sub-regulatory threshold to obtain a workable positive class and (ii) defining exceedance on a single daily grab value rather than an average — both of which support the legitimacy of our 'daily max >= 10 mg/L' construction, while also showing that shifting the threshold is a normal and defensible modeling choice rather than a corruption of the target.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: threshold set at 0.5x BAV; resulting exceedance base rates 26.9% (Chicago) and 33.6% (San Diego) — strikingly close to our violation base rate of 0.263

tier3_unverified.claim: EXTERNAL BENCHMARK for what 'good' exceedance sensitivity looks like in published environmental-threshold models: the paper's literature summary reports model sensitivity of 27-65% at Great Lakes sites and 28-30% at California beaches, with specificity typically 85-99%; the authors also note 'model sensitivity was generally better in models of FIB at rivers ... than at coastal waters.' In their own results, 'only four of the 12 models had sensitivity above 0.70.' CALIBRATION FOR OUR NUMBERS: our LOFO recall of 0.524 at a 10% false-alarm rate (i.e. specificity 0.90) sits INSIDE the upper half of that published band, and our AUC 0.820 exceeds every AUC in this paper (max 0.733, achieved with same-region training). The high-recall deployment setting (beta=2, recall 0.864, 59% false alarms) trades specificity far below the 0.85-0.99 the FIB literature holds; that is a defensible public-health choice but is out of line with published practice and should be presented as an explicit cost-sensitive decision, not as a performance claim.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: prior-literature sensitivity 27-65% (Great Lakes), 28-30% (California beaches), specificity 85-99%; this paper's own max AUC 0.733
tier3_unverified.nBasins: unknown for the summarized prior studies (aggregated from a literature table spanning Great Lakes and California beach studies); the paper's own results are from 33 beaches

tier3_unverified.claim: NEGATIVE RESULTS worth heeding before we spend effort: (i) CORAL (correlation-alignment, an UNSUPERVISED domain-adaptation method needing only unlabeled target features — the one family that WOULD be legal for our deployment target) 'never improved performance' over plain zero-shot generalization in any transfer direction; (ii) class-imbalance oversampling via SMOTE and ADASYN showed 'significant underperformance.' Implication for us: the deployment-legal adaptation methods were exactly the ones that failed, and the methods that worked were the deployment-illegal supervised ones. Also note their feature set (12 features) INCLUDED 3-day and 7-day cumulative precipitation and binary any-rain flags, which were useful there — but that is a coastal FIB system with hours-scale response, not a tile-drained agricultural nitrate system, so it is not evidence against our own rolling-precipitation failure (lofo_r2 0.013 vs 0.003). The authors' stated limitation is that they did not incorporate physical site characteristics (beach slope, pollutant sources, bathymetry) that might explain WHICH source sites transfer — the direct analogue of our missing tile-drainage-density and static between-site information.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: CORAL: zero improvement over baseline generalization in all directions; SMOTE/ADASYN: 'significant underperformance'

tier3_unverified.claim: Two identical-model in situ UV-Vis spectrophotometers (s::can spectro::lyser) installed side-by-side in the same stream disagreed substantially on sub-daily NITRATE structure: Pearson r between the two sensors' deviations-from-background was only 0.429 (NF site), 0.454 (SHA) and 0.813 (TTP) while in parallel position, whereas for dissolved organic carbon the same paired sensors agreed at r > 0.98 (p < 0.001) at all three sites. Implication for a daily-max nitrate target: the WITHIN-DAY component of a UV-Vis nitrate record is only weakly reproducible between instruments, so a daily maximum inherits instrument-specific noise that a daily mean or median would average out. Study: 4 tropical headwater/mixed catchments in Kenya (27-36 km2 sub-catchments plus a 1021 km2 outlet), 5-year record (Nov 2014-Oct 2019), 10-minute sampling.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: nitrate inter-sensor r = 0.43-0.81 vs DOC r > 0.98 in parallel position; during shading treatment nitrate r = 0.657 (NF), 0.505 (SHA), 0.236 (TTP) vs DOC r > 0.8 at all sites
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 4 catchments (3 nested sub-catchments 27-36 km2 + 1021 km2 outlet), Kenya; mobile-sensor comparison at 3 of the 4 sites

tier3_unverified.claim: Physically moving or shading one of two co-located UV-Vis sensors changed the measured diurnal nitrate pattern, but NOT in a consistent direction: shading reduced the nitrate amplitude at NF, produced lower minima at SHA and TTP, increasing sensor depth reduced amplitude at TTP but had no visible effect at SHA, and changing orientation at NF reduced amplitude of both nitrate and DOC while at TTP it left nitrate essentially unchanged. The authors conclude the observed diurnal patterns 'are not (solely) caused by natural processes' and that incident solar radiation reaching the measurement window is a likely but unproven interferent. This is a falsifiable statement that sub-daily UV-Vis nitrate structure is partly a deployment-geometry artefact rather than a biogeochemical signal.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: no consistent sign of effect across sites; qualitative amplitude and phase shifts (a ~6 h phase shift appeared at SHA after 18 Nov 2017 and persisted through depth change and shading)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 3 sites instrumented with a paired mobile sensor (NF, TTP, SHA); each treatment >= 3 days, parallel phase >= 2 weeks

tier3_unverified.claim: The manufacturer-stated accuracy of the s::can spectro::lyser nitrate measurement at 5 mm optical path length is '±2% + 0.2 mg N L−1' over a 0-60 mg N L−1 range, and the authors explicitly warn against interpreting diurnal patterns 'when the diurnal variations are of the same order of magnitude as sensor accuracy or resolution.' This sets a quantitative decision rule for whether a daily-maximum target is defensible: it is defensible only when within-day amplitude materially exceeds ~0.2 mg N/L plus 2% of the reading (i.e. ~0.4 mg N/L at 10 mg N/L). At the 10 mg/L nitrate MCL, ±2%+0.2 implies roughly ±0.4 mg N/L instrument uncertainty on any single reading, meaning site-days whose daily max falls within ~0.4 mg/L of the 10 mg/L threshold have effectively coin-flip label assignment.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: ±2% + 0.2 mg N/L nitrate accuracy; 220-720 nm, 2.5 nm resolution, 5 mm path length, 10-min measurement interval

tier3_unverified.claim: Published diurnal nitrate amplitudes compiled by this paper span three orders of magnitude across streams: 0.01-0.15 mg N L−1 in temperate and subtropical rivers in the US, Spain and the UK; 0.4-0.6 mg N L−1 in other UK rivers; and 1.5 mg N L−1 in a Mediterranean headwater stream; the Kenyan study's own amplitudes were up to 0.25 mg N L−1 (sensor B, low flow) and < 0.02 mg N L−1 during high flow. This quantifies the maximum possible divergence between a daily-MAXIMUM and a daily-MEAN nitrate target: in the typical temperate agricultural case the gap is roughly 0.005-0.3 mg N/L, i.e. small relative to a 10 mg/L threshold, but in the worst documented case (1.5 mg N/L amplitude) daily-max could exceed daily-mean by ~0.75 mg N/L, which is enough to flip exceedance labels near the threshold.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: diurnal nitrate amplitude 0.01-0.15 mg N/L (US/Spain/UK), 0.4-0.6 mg N/L (UK rivers), 1.5 mg N/L (Mediterranean headwater), <=0.25 mg N/L (this study, low flow), <0.02 mg N/L (this study, high flow)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: literature compilation across ~6 cited studies plus the 4 Kenyan catchments; individual study n not stated in this paper

tier3_unverified.claim: Diurnal amplitude in nitrate decreased monotonically with discharge class at all four Kenyan sites, becoming 'barely discernible' with mean deviations from background < 0.02 mg N L−1 during high flow (Qd > Q30), while background nitrate concentration INCREASED with discharge at SHA (0.52 -> 0.89 -> 1.30 mg N/L), TTP (1.17 -> 1.74 -> 2.21) and OUT (0.65 -> 0.84 -> 0.99) across low/medium/high flow. For an exceedance-prediction target this means the daily-max-minus-daily-mean gap is SMALLEST exactly on the high-flow days when concentrations (and therefore exceedance risk in a transport-limited agricultural system) are highest — so choosing daily max over daily mean should have least effect on the positive class and most effect on low-flow negatives.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: high-flow diurnal deviation < 0.02 mg N/L vs up to 0.25 mg N/L at low flow; background nitrate rises 0.52 -> 1.30 mg N/L (SHA) and 1.17 -> 2.21 mg N/L (TTP) from low to high flow
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 4 catchments, Kenya; flow classes defined by Q70 and Q30 exceedance percentiles of mean daily discharge

tier3_unverified.claim: The paper reports that multiple prior studies establish turbidity thresholds above which UV-Vis sensors cannot provide valid nitrate measurements — cited as > 80 FTU, > 300-450 FTU, and > 1000 NTU depending on the study — and notes this is 'especially problematic' where rainfall events cause short sharp turbidity spikes. Because high-turbidity storm periods coincide with the runoff events that drive nitrate exceedance, this predicts a systematic, non-random measurement gap or bias in sensor-derived daily maxima precisely on the highest-risk days. Testable on the Iowa dataset directly: co-located turbidity exists at 61 of 85 sites, so one can check whether nitrate observations are preferentially missing, flagged, or biased on days exceeding these turbidity levels, and whether the daily-max label is disproportionately unreliable on those days.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: turbidity invalidity thresholds for UV-Vis nitrate: >80 FTU, >300-450 FTU, >1000 NTU across three cited studies
tier3_unverified.nBasins: not-applicable (threshold values cited from Huebsch et al. 2015 HESS, Kamari et al. 2018 J. Hydrol., Lee et al. 2015 Biogeosciences)

tier3_unverified.claim: The 10 mg/L nitrate threshold used as the project's violation target is, in federal regulation, a drinking-water Maximum Contaminant Level expressed AS NITROGEN: the 40 CFR 141.62(b) table reads '(7) Nitrate | 10 (as Nitrogen)', '(8) Nitrite | 1 (as Nitrogen)', '(9) Total Nitrate and Nitrite | 10 (as Nitrogen)'. A sensor reporting nitrate as NO3 ion rather than NO3-N differs by a factor of 4.43, so the label definition is falsifiable by checking IWQIS/USGS parameter units against the CFR basis.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: MCL = 10 mg/L as N; 4.43x conversion risk if units are NO3 ion

tier3_unverified.claim: Nitrate is one of the few Safe Drinking Water Act contaminants whose compliance is determined on a SINGLE sample rather than a running annual average: 40 CFR 141.23(i)(3) states 'Compliance with the maximum contaminant levels for nitrate and nitrate is determined based on one sample if the levels of these contaminants are below the MCLs.' This is regulatory support for an event-level (daily) binary framing rather than a smoothed or annual-average target, and is consistent with the project's finding that 3-day/7-day rolling smoothed targets performed worse.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: n=1 sample compliance basis for nitrate, versus annual-average basis used for other inorganic contaminants in 141.23(i)(1)-(2)

tier3_unverified.claim: The operative regulatory exceedance statistic for nitrate is the MEAN OF TWO samples, not a single reading: 40 CFR 141.23(f)(2) requires that 'Where nitrate or nitrite sampling results indicate an exceedance of the maximum contaminant level, the system shall take a confirmation sample within 24 hours', and 141.23(i)(3) continues 'If the levels of nitrate and/or nitrite exceed the MCLs in the initial sample, a confirmation sample is required ... and compliance shall be determined based on the average of the initial and confirmation samples.' The regulatory analogue of the project's target is therefore closer to a 24-hour mean conditional on an initial exceedance than to a daily maximum, implying the current daily-max label is systematically MORE permissive of positives than the regulatory statistic.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: averaging window = 24 hours, 2 samples; daily-max label is an upper bound on the regulatory 2-sample mean

tier3_unverified.claim: A second regulatory decision threshold exists at 50 percent of the MCL (5 mg/L as N), which triggers increased monitoring frequency: 40 CFR 141.23(d)(3) provides that a surface water system may reduce sampling 'to annually if all analytical results from four consecutive quarters are <50 percent of the MCL. A surface water system shall return to quarterly monitoring if any one sample is >=50 percent of the MCL', and 141.23(d)(2) imposes quarterly monitoring on groundwater systems 'for at least one year following any one sample in which the concentration is >=50 percent of the MCL.' This means a 5 mg/L classification target is a genuine, citable regulatory decision boundary and not an arbitrary alternative threshold, and it would have a substantially higher base rate than the current 0.263, plausibly improving the between-site signal-to-noise the project is short of.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: regulatory trigger at 5 mg/L as N = 50% of MCL; drives quarterly vs annual monitoring

tier3_unverified.claim: The federal nitrate MCL applies to TREATED water at the entry point to the distribution system, not to ambient raw stream water: 40 CFR 141.23(a)(2) requires that 'Surface water systems shall take a minimum of one sample at every entry point to the distribution system after any application of treatment or in the distribution system at a point which is representative of each source after treatment.' Applying the 10 mg/L MCL to raw in-stream nitrate at an arbitrary map pin is therefore an analogy to a drinking-water standard, not a regulatory exceedance in the CFR sense, and any product framing must say so; the ambient-stream regulatory instruments (state water quality standards, 303(d) listing, TMDLs) are not defined in 40 CFR 141.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: compliance point = post-treatment entry point; zero CFR 141 provisions apply to ambient streams

tier3_unverified.claim: 40 CFR 141.23 establishes a QUARTERLY (surface water) or ANNUAL (groundwater) nitrate sampling regime -- '(d)(1) Community and non-transient, non-community water systems served by groundwater systems shall monitor annually beginning January 1, 1993; systems served by surface water shall monitor quarterly beginning January 1, 1993' -- and contains NO provision addressing continuous, high-frequency, or daily sensor measurements. This is direct evidence of the sampling-frequency bias problem: the regulatory record against which any 'violation' rate would historically be judged is built from 4 grab samples per year, whereas the project's label is built from ~365 daily sensor maxima per year, so the project's 0.263 base rate is not comparable to any published regulatory exceedance rate.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 4 samples/year (surface water) or 1/year (groundwater) regulatory frequency vs ~365 daily maxima in the project label; ~90x frequency mismatch

tier3_unverified.claim: Iowa's 10 mg/L nitrate-nitrogen criterion is a DESIGNATED-USE-SPECIFIC criterion applying ONLY to Class C waters ('source of a water supply'); Iowa has NO nitrate criterion for any aquatic-life class. The Table 6 criteria matrix lists 'nitrate-nitrogen (mg/L)' as 'none' for Class A1/A2/A3 (swimmable), BWW1, BWW2 & BWW3, BCW1, BCW2, BLW and Class HH, with the single value '10' under 'Class C: source of a water supply'. Narrative: 'The Iowa Water Quality Standards identify this 10 mg/L MCL as the water quality criterion to protect surface waters used as a source of a municipal water supply. At concentrations seen in surface waters, nitrate is not believed to be toxic to aquatic life; thus, there are no water quality criteria in the Iowa Water Quality Standards that apply to aquatic life uses.' IMPLICATION FOR THE ARBITRARY-MAP-PIN PRODUCT: a 'violation' prediction at an arbitrary Iowa pin has NO regulatory meaning unless that segment is Class C designated; elsewhere the label is merely a physically-defined threshold exceedance, and the product must say so rather than implying a regulatory exceedance.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 10 mg/L as N; applies to exactly 1 of 9 designated-use classes in Table 6; nitrate criterion = 'none' for all 6 aquatic-life classes

tier3_unverified.claim: The regulatory unit of nitrate exceedance in Iowa is NOT a single day and NOT a single sample — it is the FRACTION of samples exceeding 10 mg/L over a THREE-YEAR assessment period, tested for significance against a 10% rule at >90% confidence. Verbatim: 'Data for inorganics (i.e., nitrate) in the raw water source: If, over the three-year assessment period, significantly more than 10% of the samples violate Iowa's Class C criterion for nitrate for drinking water use (i.e., the maximum contaminant level (MCL)), impairment of the Class C uses will be identified. The methodology of Lin et al. (2000) (Table 11) will be used to determine whether significantly more than 10% of the samples exceed the MCL.' Contrast the co-located atrazine rule, which DOES use an averaging period: 'moving annual average values for the three-year assessment period will be compared to the respective Class C criterion' — Iowa deliberately uses frequency-of-exceedance for nitrate and a moving annual average for atrazine. DIRECT RELEVANCE TO THE CENTRAL PROBLEM: the regulatorily meaningful quantity is a site's long-run exceedance RATE, precisely the between-site term the project predicts worst (between_rate_r2 0.24 vs macro_auc 0.90). A model that is 'a good timer, a mediocre site-ranker' is optimized for the wrong functional of the distribution relative to how the regulator defines the problem.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 3-year assessment window; 10%-of-samples threshold; >90% confidence level; nitrate uses frequency-of-exceedance while atrazine uses a moving annual average

tier3_unverified.claim: Iowa's nitrate assessment outcome is THREE-CLASS, not binary. Table 10, for 'Waterbodies designated for use as a source of potable water (=raw water source)' with 'Nitrate, chloride, fluoride data', defines: FULLY SUPPORTED = '<10% of the samples violate the nitrate, chloride, and fluoride maximum contaminant levels (MCLs) (90% CL)'; PARTIALLY SUPPORTED = '>10% to <25% of the samples violate the MCL(s) (90% CL)'; NOT SUPPORTED = '>25% of the samples exceed the MCL(s)'. Minimum sample sizes apply: Table 10 requires 'A minimum of 10 samples is needed' for conventional-parameter assessments and 'A minimum of 10 samples is needed for Fully Supported' for toxic parameters. IMPLICATION: the decision-relevant output is a site-level exceedance-RATE estimate binned at the 10% and 25% cut points. This suggests evaluating the model on whether it places an unseen basin in the correct <10% / 10-25% / >25% bin — a regulator-aligned test of the between-site term that is feasible at n=19 independent basin families, because it needs 19 rate estimates rather than 160k row-level predictions.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: cut points at 10% and 25% of samples exceeding; minimum n=10 samples for an assessment

tier3_unverified.claim: Iowa DNR's binomial small-sample correction (Lin et al. 2000, as tabulated by NDEQ 2006 in Table 11) specifies exact exceedance counts required to declare impairment at >90% confidence: n=10 requires 3 exceedances (CL 0.930); n=11 requires 3 (0.910); n=12 requires 4 (0.974); n=19 requires 5 (0.965); n=25 requires 5 (0.902); n=40 requires 7 (0.900); n=50 requires 9 (0.942); n=75 requires 12 (0.931); n=100 requires 15 (0.927). The required exceedance FRACTION is far above 10% at small n (3/10 = 30%, 5/25 = 20%) and converges toward 15% only at n=100. OPERATIONAL VALUE: an agency-sanctioned uncertainty rule that can be applied directly to the project's per-site sensor records and to model-predicted exceedance rates. It quantifies how many observations a site needs before its exceedance rate is even estimable — relevant because the project's sites vary greatly in record length, and short-record sites carry rate estimates the regulator itself would refuse to act on.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: n=10 -> 3 exceedances (CL 0.930); n=25 -> 5 (0.902); n=50 -> 9 (0.942); n=100 -> 15 (0.927); effective required fraction 30% at n=10 falling to 15% at n=100

tier3_unverified.claim: Iowa DNR has an EXPLICIT precedent for reducing continuous (sub-daily) sensor data to a DAILY BINARY violation flag and then applying the 10% rule over days — but only for dissolved oxygen, and with replication requirements the project's nitrate target does not impose. Attachment 6 states grab-sample methods 'are not directly applicable' to 24-hour sensor data, so a separate methodology was built: 'a violation would be a day where levels of dissolved oxygen failed to remain above the 16-hour criterion for at least 16 hours' or 'a day (24-hour period) when the dissolved oxygen falls below the 24-hour criterion.' Impairment then requires: 'Based on a 28-day deployment of continuous dissolved oxygen monitoring equipment, a Section 303(d) impairment of designated aquatic life uses will be identified if any of the following conditions occurs during each of two 28-day monitoring periods during different years within a five-year period: Significantly greater than 10% of the days monitored have levels of dissolved oxygen that fail to meet the [criterion]', using the same Lin et al. (2000) binomial test. TWO IMPLICATIONS: (1) the project's 'daily statistic -> binary day flag' construction matches the agency's own reduction of continuous sensor data, supporting the target's construction; (2) the agency requires the >10%-of-days condition to recur in TWO DIFFERENT YEARS within five years before listing, explicitly guarding against single-year weather anomalies — a robustness criterion the per-day label does not encode, and one reinforced by the document's rationale for three-year windows, which 'helps address the problem of weather-related year-to-year fluctuations in water quality.'
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 28-day deployment; >10% of monitored days in violation; must recur in 2 different years within a 5-year period; Lin et al. binomial at >90% CL

tier3_unverified.claim: The 10 mg/L number Iowa applies to RAW stream water is borrowed verbatim from a FINISHED (treated, delivered) drinking-water standard, with no treatment, blending, or dilution adjustment anywhere in the methodology. Verbatim: 'the EPA recommends that nitrate levels in water delivered by a public water supply to consumers should not exceed a maximum contaminant level (MCL) of 10 mg/L as nitrogen. The Iowa Water Quality Standards identify this 10 mg/L MCL as the water quality criterion to protect surface waters used as a source of a municipal water supply.' Raw and finished water stay on separate tracks: raw-water data feed the Table 10 / 10%-rule process, while 'Impairments related to the quality of finished (treated) water will be determined through review of [the] annual Iowa DNR public drinking water program compliance reports', keyed to closures and advisories ('One drinking water advisory lasting 30 days or less per year' = partially supported; 'more than 30 days per year' = not supported). SEPARATE CALIBRATION DATUM, useful as an external base-rate check on the project's 0.263 violation rate: 'the median level of nitrate+nitrite in the approximately 9,500 samples collected from 2000 through 2009 as part of Iowa DNR's ambient stream/river water quality monitoring network is 5.8 parts per million (ppm). Seventy-five percent of the samples had nitrate levels greater than 3.0 ppm.' That grab-sample median of 5.8 mg/L sits well below 10 mg/L, and the project's 26.3% daily-max exceedance rate on continuous sensors should be reconciled against it — the gap plausibly reflects daily-MAXIMUM vs grab-sample statistics plus sensor-site selection toward high-nitrate agricultural basins, a testable sampling-frequency-bias hypothesis this source raises but does not resolve.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: MCL 10 mg/L as N defined on delivered/treated water, adopted unchanged as the raw-source criterion; Iowa DNR ambient network 2000-2009 median nitrate+nitrite = 5.8 ppm over ~9,500 samples, 75th percentile > 3.0 ppm
tier3_unverified.nBasins: ~9,500 grab samples from the Iowa DNR ambient stream/river monitoring network, 2000-2009; number of distinct sites/basins not stated in the source

tier3_unverified.claim: Baggio & Muzy (2026, arXiv:2605.31079) directly test the exact methodological fork this project faces — direct binary classification of threshold exceedance (their model M1, MLP with binary cross-entropy, one model per threshold) versus modeling the full conditional distribution of the continuous target and integrating its tail (their M2, a neural network emitting parameters of a Multifractal-Rice distribution for wind speed and a zero-inflated lognormal for hourly rainfall) — and report that M2 was better or equal everywhere tested: 'metrics associated with model M2 are consistently better than the ones obtained with the classification approach M1', with no reported case where direct classification beat the distributional approach. Data: MeteoNet, southeastern France, 2016-2018, 278 wind stations and 268 rainfall stations, ~4.1e6 samples.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Direction only; paper reports results in log-scale figures, not tables. Peirce Skill Score for M2 rises as exceedance becomes rarer while M1's PSS 'sharply deteriorates when p->0'; Brier Skill Score shows 'faster degradation of BSS1 with respect to BSS2'. No exact PSS/BSS/CSI/HSS numbers are tabulated in the paper.
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: random-split (85/10/5 train/val/test) blocked by calendar day with a 17:00 UTC cutoff to prevent temporal autocorrelation leakage; NOT spatially held out — models are trained and tested on the same stations, so these numbers are NOT comparable to our LOFO 0.820
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 278 wind stations / 268 rainfall stations (meteorological stations, not basins)

tier3_unverified.claim: The mechanism Baggio & Muzy give for the distributional approach's advantage is a sample-size argument that applies directly to our 26.3% base rate and, more sharply, to any rarer threshold we might adopt: for direct binary classification 'the effective amount of information used to calibrate M1 parameters is pN instead of N', where p is the exceedance base rate and N the number of samples, whereas the distributional model 'can effectively learn the parameters of the conditional distribution even from moderate and mild intensity events'. Implication for us: our 160,074 site-days at p=0.263 give the classifier ~42,000 effective informative rows, while a regression/distributional head uses all 160,074 — but the gap the paper documents is largest as p->0 and is small at moderate p, so at p=0.263 the predicted gain is modest.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Theoretical asymptotic errors: E1 ~ p^(rho^2/(2+rho^2)) [ln(1/p)]^(-1/(2+rho^2)) versus E2 ~ p^((2+2rho^2)/(2+rho^2)) [ln(1/p)]^((1+rho^2)/(2+rho^2)), where rho^2 is the noise-to-signal ratio; the M2 advantage widens as p->0 and the two are comparable at moderate p
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: random-split (day-blocked), same stations in train and test

tier3_unverified.claim: Baggio & Muzy report that the choice of parametric family for the conditional distribution matters far less than getting its first two moments right: 'The specific parametric shape of the chosen distribution plays a secondary role compared to accurately capturing predictable shifts in its bulk properties (i.e., mean and variance).' They interpret this as extreme weather being driven by conditional displacement of the whole distribution rather than by intrinsic tail behaviour. For this project this is a falsifiable, cheap-to-test prediction: a heteroscedastic two-head model (predicted mean AND predicted variance of daily-max nitrate) integrated above 10 mg/L should recover most of the benefit, without needing an exotic tail distribution — and, critically, the between-site deficit we have (between_r2 0.21) is exactly a failure to place the conditional MEAN of an unseen basin, which this framing says is the dominant term.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Qualitative claim stated by the authors; no ablation numbers across distribution families are quoted in the text retrieved
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: random-split (day-blocked), same stations in train and test

tier3_unverified.claim: Baggio & Muzy explicitly considered and REJECTED extreme value theory for this task: they note that 'Many extreme weather nowcasting approaches integrate Extreme Value Theory (EVT) directly into modeling' and discuss the Peaks-Over-Threshold / Generalized Pareto Distribution route, but decline to use it because threshold selection introduces 'a notoriously difficult bias-variance trade-off', pursuing full-distribution parametric modeling instead. This is a documented negative-leaning judgement against POT/GPD for operational exceedance forecasting at moderate exceedance rates, and it is directly relevant here: at a 26.3% base rate our 10 mg/L violations are NOT in the EVT tail regime at all, so peaks-over-threshold machinery is unlikely to be the right tool for this project's primary target.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Not applicable — methodological rejection, no comparative numbers reported

tier3_unverified.claim: MAJOR LIMITATION FOR OUR DEPLOYMENT TARGET: Baggio & Muzy's evaluation is entirely in-station interpolation, not spatial transfer. Their exceedance thresholds are defined per-station ('thresholds Qp are calculated station-wise', i.e. as station-specific empirical quantiles rather than a single absolute physical threshold), and the paper contains no experiment applying a trained model to a station absent from training. Their protocol therefore measures WHEN exceedance happens at a known site — precisely the 'good timer' capability this project already has (within_r2 0.42, macro_auc 0.90) — and provides NO evidence about the between-site absolute-level problem that constitutes essentially all of our remaining headroom (between_r2 0.21, between_rate_r2 0.24). Their skill numbers must not be compared to our LOFO 0.820 AUC.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: No spatially-held-out results reported
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 278 wind stations / 268 rainfall stations, all seen in training

tier3_unverified.claim: Baggio & Muzy's evaluation-metric set for threshold exceedance is proper scoring rules (Brier score and logarithmic score, reported as skill scores BSS relative to a climatological reference) PLUS threshold-dependent deterministic skill scores (Peirce Skill Score, Critical Success Index, Heidke Skill Score) evaluated as a function of the exceedance probability p — not AUC/PR-AUC. Because PSS, CSI and HSS are computed against a climatological/base-rate reference, they are far more comparable across studies with different base rates than raw AUC is; this project currently reports AUC 0.820, PR-AUC 0.634 (2.41x lift) and Brier 0.137 but no BSS, PSS, CSI or HSS, which is a concrete reason our numbers cannot be benchmarked against this literature. Adding BSS against a base-rate-0.263 climatology and PSS/CSI/HSS at the operating point would make our LOFO results directly citable against exceedance-forecasting papers.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Metric-choice claim, no performance number attached; our Brier 0.137 against a 0.263-base-rate climatological Brier of 0.263*0.737 = 0.1938 implies BSS ~ 0.293 (derived here, not from the paper)
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: random-split (day-blocked), same stations in train and test
